title: 22. Interview: Block Storage
summary: Interview Q&A for Block Storage — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Block Storage interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between ephemeral block storage and persistent block storage, and when would you choose each?
**Answer:** Ephemeral block storage is local to the host running the instance — it is the NVMe SSDs physically inside the server — and its lifetime is tied to the instance: stop or terminate the instance and the data is gone. Persistent block storage (EBS, Azure Disk, GCP Persistent Disk) is network-attached and lives independently of the instance, so you can stop, restart, or migrate the instance without losing data. Ephemeral storage is faster (no network hop, direct PCIe), cheaper (no replication overhead), and ideal for scratch space, caches, swap, and intermediate computation results that can be regenerated. Persistent storage is the right choice for anything that must survive an instance failure — databases, boot volumes, application state. The pattern for high-performance databases is often a hybrid: the WAL on persistent EBS io2 for durability, and the temp tablespace on ephemeral instance-store NVMe for speed. AWS's `i3` and `i4` instance types provide large ephemeral NVMe for exactly this use case. The architectural rule: if you can recompute the data, ephemeral is fine; if you cannot, persistent is mandatory.
**Visual:**
```
ephemeral:    instance host NVMe (PCIe)  -> 1-2 TB, fast, dies with instance
persistent:   network-attached EBS        -> survives stop/terminate/migrate
hybrid DB:    WAL on EBS io2 (durable) + temp on instance-store NVMe (fast)
```

### Q2. How does EBS achieve 99.9% (or 99.999% for io2) durability, and what are its failure modes?
**Answer:** EBS durability comes from synchronous replication: every write to a volume is acknowledged only after it has been persisted to two storage nodes in different racks within the same AZ. This protects against single-node failure (the standby has the data), single-rack power loss (the replica is in a different rack), and individual SSD failures (the storage node's own RAID rebuilds transparently). The 99.9% durability figure for gp2/gp3 means you expect to lose one volume per 1,000 per year — not great for irreplaceable data. io2 Block Express raises this to 99.999% (one volume per 100,000 per year) via additional replication and stronger checksums, which is why databases use it. The failure modes that replication does NOT protect against: AZ outage (both replicas are in the same AZ — for cross-AZ durability you need snapshots to S3 or cross-AZ volume replication); storage-node firmware bugs that silently corrupt both replicas (rare but has happened); and user error (deleting the volume). The defense against AZ-level and user-error failure is snapshots: EBS snapshots are stored in S3 (which itself has 11 nines durability across 3+ AZs), so a daily snapshot gives you a cross-AZ recovery point. The rule: replication protects against hardware failure; snapshots protect against AZ outage and user error.
**Visual:**
```
write -> storage node 1 (rack A) + storage node 2 (rack B) -- sync, <1ms
         protects against: single node, single rack, single SSD
         does NOT protect against: AZ outage, user delete, fw bug
snapshot -> S3 (cross-AZ, 11 nines) -- async, daily
            protects against: AZ outage, user delete
```

### Q3. Why is block storage single-attach by default, and what does EBS Multi-Attach actually enable?
**Answer:** Block storage is single-attach because the filesystem on top of it (ext4, XFS, NTFS) assumes exclusive access — it maintains in-memory caches of metadata and data that would be corrupted if a second writer modified the disk underneath. If two instances mounted the same ext4 volume and both wrote, they would each see a stale view of the metadata, overwrite each other's changes, and silently corrupt the filesystem within seconds. EBS Multi-Attach allows up to 16 Nitro-based instances in the same AZ to attach the same io2 volume concurrently, but it does NOT solve the multi-writer problem — it only enables readers and a single coordinated writer. The legitimate use cases are: cluster quorum disks (where only one node writes at a time, enforced by a distributed lock manager like in Oracle RAC); shared read-only data (where many instances read the same dataset and writes happen via a separate workflow); and active-passive failover (where the standby mounts the volume but does not write until failover). For true multi-writer shared storage, you need a cluster filesystem (OCFS2, GFS2) or a distributed filesystem (Ceph RBD with locking), which adds significant complexity. The rule of thumb: if you need multi-writer shared storage, you probably want file storage or a database, not multi-attached block storage.
**Visual:**
```
default:  volume -> attached to 1 instance (exclusive writer)
multi-attach: volume -> up to 16 instances, BUT:
              - filesystem still assumes exclusive access -> silent corruption
              - legit uses: quorum disk, read-only shared, active-passive
              - NOT legit: two app servers writing the same files
need multi-writer? -> use file storage (NFS/SMB) or a real DB
```

### Q4. What is the difference between IOPS, throughput, and latency as block-storage performance metrics, and which limits which?
**Answer:** IOPS (input/output operations per second) is the count of individual block operations — a 4KB read is one IOP, a 256KB read is also one IOP (below the max block size). Throughput is bytes per second — IOPS × block size, capped at the volume's throughput limit. Latency is the time from issuing an I/O to its completion, dominated by the storage medium (NVMe ~0.1ms, network overhead ~0.5–2ms in EBS). The relationship is: a volume has three independent caps (IOPS, throughput MB/s, and per-I/O latency), and the actual performance is bounded by whichever cap you hit first. For small random I/O (4KB OLTP), you hit the IOPS cap first — a gp3 volume at 3,000 IOPS does 12 MB/s of 4KB reads, far below its 125 MB/s throughput cap. For large sequential I/O (1MB analytics scans), you hit the throughput cap first — 125 MB/s / 1MB = 125 IOPS, far below the 3,000 IOPS cap. The architectural implication: size IOPS for your random workload (databases need 3,000–16,000 IOPS), size throughput for your sequential workload (analytics needs 250–1,000 MB/s), and remember that latency is mostly fixed by the medium — you cannot buy lower latency, only more IOPS and throughput. EBS gp3 lets you tune IOPS and throughput independently of capacity, which is why it replaced gp2.
**Visual:**
```
small random (4KB):  3000 IOPS x 4KB = 12 MB/s  -> IOPS-bound (typical DB)
large seq (1MB):     125 IOPS x 1MB = 125 MB/s   -> throughput-bound (analytics)
latency:             fixed by medium (NVMe 0.1ms + net 0.5-2ms)
gp3: tune IOPS and MB/s independently of capacity
```

### Q5. How do EBS snapshots work, and what is the difference between a crash-consistent and application-consistent snapshot?
**Answer:** EBS snapshots are point-in-time, block-level copies stored in S3. The mechanism is copy-on-write: when you trigger a snapshot, EBS briefly pauses writes, records the current state of every block's metadata, and resumes I/O; from that point forward, every block that is overwritten on the live volume is first copied to the snapshot store in S3. The result is a logically complete snapshot stored as a series of block deltas in S3, and you pay only for the changed blocks (so the first snapshot is full-size, subsequent snapshots are incremental). Snapshots are crash-consistent by default — they capture the on-disk state at the moment of the pause, which means the filesystem is in a state as if the power had been pulled mid-write. For a database, this can mean torn writes (a transaction half-applied) and the database must run recovery on first boot from the snapshot. Application-consistent snapshots coordinate with the application: you flush the database's WAL (e.g., `pg_backup_start()` / `pg_backup_stop()` in PostgreSQL), freeze writes, snapshot, then resume — the resulting snapshot is recoverable without replay. AWS provides the Data Lifecycle Manager and AWS Backup services to automate application-consistent snapshots via pre/post scripts. The rule: for filesystems and databases with WAL replay, crash-consistent is fine; for databases without WAL or for stateful apps that cannot replay, use application-consistent.
**Visual:**
```
snapshot trigger: pause writes -> record block metadata -> resume I/O
                  COW: every subsequent overwrite -> copy old block to S3
crash-consistent:  on-disk state, like power pull (DB replays WAL on boot)
app-consistent:    flush WAL -> freeze -> snap -> resume (no replay needed)
storage:           first snap full, later snaps incremental (deltas only)
```

### Q6. Why does EBS io2 Block Express exist, and what workload requires it versus gp3?
**Answer:** gp3 is the general-purpose SSD tier — up to 16,000 IOPS, 1,000 MB/s throughput, 99.9% durability, ~$0.08/GB-month. It covers 95% of workloads: web servers, app servers, dev/test databases, small to medium production databases. io2 Block Express is the premium tier — up to 256,000 IOPS, 4,000 MB/s throughput, 99.999% durability, sub-millisecond latency, ~$0.125/GB-month. It exists for the workloads that gp3 cannot serve: large mission-critical databases (SAP HANA, Oracle RAC, large PostgreSQL/MySQL), where the IOPS ceiling of gp3 caps transaction throughput; data warehouses doing thousands of concurrent scans; and any workload where 99.9% durability is insufficient (one volume per 1,000 per year is too risky for a financial ledger). The 99.999% durability is achieved via additional replicas and stronger end-to-end checksums. The IOPS ceiling matters because a busy 50TB PostgreSQL database doing random 4KB OLTP reads at 60K IOPS saturates gp3 — you either shard across multiple gp3 volumes (operational complexity) or use one io2 Block Express volume (simplicity at higher cost). The rule: start with gp3, monitor `VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps` and `VolumeQueueLength`, and only upgrade to io2 when you are consistently hitting gp3's caps.
**Visual:**
```
gp3:    16K IOPS, 1GB/s, 99.9% durable, $0.08/GB   -> 95% of workloads
io2 BE: 256K IOPS, 4GB/s, 99.999% durable, $0.125/GB -> mission-critical DBs
upgrade trigger: VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps near cap, queue length > 1
```

### Q7. How does block storage interact with the guest OS's filesystem, and why does this matter for performance?
**Answer:** Block storage exposes raw blocks; the guest OS formats them with a filesystem (ext4, XFS, NTFS) that adds metadata (inodes, block bitmaps, journal) and provides file abstractions. The filesystem's behavior — block size, allocation strategy, journaling mode, and caching — directly determines how the underlying block storage is used. For example, ext4 with a 4KB block size means every 4KB file write becomes one block I/O; an XFS with 64KB extents can coalesce small writes into larger sequential I/O, which is why XFS is preferred for large databases and analytics. The journaling mode matters: `data=ordered` (the ext4 default) writes data before metadata, `data=journal` journals both (safer but ~50% slower), and `data=writeback` journals only metadata (fastest but allows torn data on crash). The guest OS also has its own page cache, which can mask block-storage latency for hot reads but adds a write-back delay that affects durability — `fsync()` must flush the page cache to the block device, which is when EBS latency actually bites. The architectural implications: choose a filesystem matched to the workload (XFS for databases, ext4 for general use, NTFS for Windows); tune the journal mode (writeback for analytics, ordered or journal for OLTP); and size the page cache to fit the working set. The interaction is why a "fast EBS volume" can still feel slow if the filesystem is misconfigured.
**Visual:**
```
block storage:  raw 4KB blocks at LBA 0..N
guest OS:       mkfs.ext4 -> inode table, journal, block bitmap
                page cache (RAM) -> masks hot reads, defers writes
write path:     app write -> page cache -> fsync -> block write -> EBS
fsync is where EBS latency bites (5-50ms depending on tier)
fs choice:      XFS for DBs (large extents), ext4 for general, NTFS for Windows
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your PostgreSQL database on a 1TB gp3 volume is hitting `VolumeQueueLength > 10` during peak hours and query latency is spiking to 500ms. How do you diagnose and fix this?
**Answer:** `VolumeQueueLength > 1` sustained means the volume is saturated — I/Os are queueing faster than the volume can serve them, and each query waits in the queue, inflating latency. The diagnosis is to check three CloudWatch metrics: `VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps` (is it at the IOPS cap?), `VolumeThroughputPercentage` (is it at the throughput cap?), and `VolumeQueueLength` (how saturated?). If `VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps` is at 3,000 (the gp3 default), the volume is IOPS-bound — typical for OLTP doing random 4KB I/O. If `VolumeThroughputPercentage` is at 100%, it's throughput-bound — typical for analytics doing large scans. The fix depends on the diagnosis. For IOPS-bound OLTP: bump gp3 IOPS from 3,000 to 16,000 (a 30-second operation, no downtime) — this is the cheapest fix and usually resolves the issue. If 16,000 IOPS is still insufficient, either migrate to io2 Block Express (256,000 IOPS, more expensive) or shard the database across multiple volumes. For throughput-bound analytics: bump gp3 throughput from 125 to 1,000 MB/s (also a 30-second operation). Beyond tuning, examine the query mix — a missing index can turn a single-row lookup into a 10,000-block sequential scan, multiplying IOPS by 1,000x. The architectural lesson: storage tuning is a stopgap; the real fix is usually query optimization or schema redesign, with EBS tuning as the cost.
**Visual:**
```
diagnose: VolumeQueueLength > 1 -> saturated
          VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps at cap -> IOPS-bound (OLTP)
          VolumeThroughputPercentage = 100% -> throughput-bound (analytics)
fix OLTP:    gp3 3000 -> 16000 IOPS (30s, no downtime)
fix analytics: gp3 125 -> 1000 MB/s
still stuck: io2 Block Express OR shard DB OR add index (root cause)
```

### Q2. You need to migrate a 10TB EBS volume from one AZ to another with minimal downtime. Walk through the approach.
**Answer:** EBS volumes are AZ-bound — you cannot "move" a volume; you must create a copy in the target AZ. The standard approach: take a snapshot of the source volume (a few minutes for the pause, then async background copy to S3 taking 30–60 minutes for 10TB depending on change rate), then create a new volume in the target AZ from the snapshot (a few seconds for the API call, but the volume "warms up" lazily as blocks are fetched from S3 on first read). For minimal downtime, use a snapshot + incremental catch-up pattern: take snapshot S1, mount the new volume in the target AZ, start the database on it, and let it run ahead of the cutover while shipping WAL deltas from the source. At cutover time, stop the source database, take a final snapshot S2 (incremental, fast since most blocks unchanged since S1), apply S2 to the target volume, restart the database on the target — total downtime is minutes, not hours. For PostgreSQL specifically, the cleaner pattern is to use logical replication (pglogical or native logical replication) to keep a standby in the target AZ continuously up to date, then promote it at cutover — downtime is seconds. The 10TB size means the initial snapshot copy to S3 is the slow part; for terabyte-scale data, always prefer continuous replication (logical or physical) over snapshot-based migration.
**Visual:**
```
naive:    snapshot 10TB to S3 (1h) -> restore in new AZ (1h) -> 2h downtime
better:   snapshot S1 (catch-up) -> mount target, replay WAL continuously
          cutover: stop source, snap S2 (incremental, fast), apply, restart
          downtime: minutes
best:     logical replication (pglogical) -> standby in target AZ
          promote at cutover -> downtime: seconds
```

### Q3. Your Cassandra cluster uses instance-store NVMe (ephemeral) for performance. An instance dies and you lose 2TB of data. How do you recover, and is this design correct?
**Answer:** The recovery depends on Cassandra's replication: if `replication_factor=3` and the lost node held one replica of each token range, the cluster still has two copies and can rebuild the lost replica by streaming from the surviving replicas. The standard recovery is to launch a replacement instance, join it to the cluster, and run `nodetool repair` (or rely on Cassandra's automatic bootstrap streaming) — the new node pulls its share of the data from the surviving replicas over the network. For 2TB, this takes 1–4 hours depending on network bandwidth and cluster load. The design — ephemeral NVMe for Cassandra — is actually correct for Cassandra's architecture: Cassandra is designed for shared-nothing, replicate-everywhere storage, and using persistent EBS would be both more expensive (EBS at 3x replication per node plus Cassandra's 3x replication = 9x storage cost) and slower (EBS adds network latency to every write). The architectural rule: for systems with native multi-node replication (Cassandra, HDFS, Kafka with replication factor 3), ephemeral storage is the right choice — you trade per-node durability for cross-node durability, which is what the system was designed for. The operational requirement is to monitor cluster health and replace failed nodes promptly; Netflix's Chaos Monkey deliberately kills instances to ensure this works. The one caveat: if you lose multiple nodes simultaneously (e.g., a rack failure), you may need backups — Cassandra backups are typically snapshots to S3 taken nightly.
**Visual:**
```
Cassandra RF=3, 3 nodes, ephemeral NVMe each
node dies -> 1 replica lost, 2 survive -> rebuild via streaming
                                 -> 1-4h, automated by nodetool repair
why ephemeral: Cassandra's replication = durability; EBS would be 9x cost
rule: native multi-node replication -> ephemeral OK
      single-node durability required -> persistent (EBS)
```

### Q4. You are running a Kafka cluster on EBS gp3 volumes. The producer throughput is capped at 200 MB/s per broker, but you expected 1,000 MB/s. What is wrong?
**Answer:** Kafka's throughput on EBS is bounded by the smaller of three limits: the volume's throughput cap, the volume's IOPS cap (for small messages), and the broker's network egress. For a gp3 volume with default 125 MB/s throughput, the cap is the volume, not Kafka — bump gp3 throughput to 1,000 MB/s (a 30-second operation). But this is only the first issue. Kafka's log architecture is append-only sequential writes, which should be throughput-bound, but the consumer reads are also sequential reads from the same volume — so the volume must support both write and read throughput simultaneously, and the 1,000 MB/s cap is shared, not per-direction. A second issue is the IOPS cap: if messages are small (1KB), 1,000 MB/s = 1,000,000 IOPS, far above gp3's 16,000 IOPS cap — so small-message Kafka is IOPS-bound, not throughput-bound. The fix for small messages is to batch (Kafka's `linger.ms` and `batch.size` settings coalesce small messages into larger writes, converting IOPS-bound to throughput-bound). A third issue is EBS's per-instance network cap: an m5.2xlarge has 2.5 Gbps network, which caps total broker throughput at ~300 MB/s regardless of EBS — you need a larger instance or ENA trunking. The lesson: Kafka performance on EBS requires matching the volume tier (gp3 throughput and IOPS), the broker config (batching), and the instance network cap.
**Visual:**
```
limit chain:  min(EBS throughput, EBS IOPS, instance network)
small msg (1KB):  1000MB/s needs 1M IOPS -> gp3 caps at 16K -> batch!
                 linger.ms=10, batch.size=64KB -> 16K IOPS x 64KB = 1GB/s
large msg (100KB): 1000MB/s = 10K IOPS -> within gp3 IOPS cap
instance net:    m5.2xlarge 2.5Gbps = 300MB/s ceiling (need bigger)
```

### Q5. Your security team requires full-disk encryption for all EBS volumes, with keys rotated annually, and zero performance impact. How do you implement this?
**Answer:** Use EBS encryption with AWS KMS, which is the native and only sensible approach. EBS encryption is transparent: when you create an encrypted volume, EBS generates a data key from a KMS customer-managed key (CMK), encrypts the volume with AES-256, and all reads/writes are decrypted/encrypted on the storage node's hardware accelerator (AWS Nitro) with negligible performance overhead — typically <1% latency increase. The encryption is invisible to the guest OS: the OS sees plaintext blocks, and the network path between the instance and the storage node carries ciphertext. Key rotation is the tricky part: KMS supports automatic annual rotation of the CMK, which rotates the master key but does NOT re-encrypt existing data — the old key version is retained and used to decrypt existing volumes, while new volumes use the new key version. To actually re-encrypt a volume with a new key (full rotation), you must create a snapshot of the volume and restore it as a new encrypted volume with the new CMK — which means a brief downtime or, for a database, a snapshot-and-restore cycle. For zero-downtime rotation, run two volumes side-by-side (old and new) and replicate via the application (e.g., PostgreSQL logical replication) — cutover when caught up. The architectural rule: KMS CMK auto-rotation is sufficient for most compliance needs (it rotates the master key annually, existing data uses old key version which is still in KMS); full data re-encryption is required only if the regulation explicitly demands it (rare).
**Visual:**
```
EBS encryption: KMS CMK -> data key -> AES-256 on Nitro HW (<1% overhead)
                guest OS sees plaintext, wire is ciphertext
CMK auto-rotation: annual master key rotation, existing data uses old version
                   new volumes use new version -> sufficient for most compliance
full re-encrypt: snapshot + restore with new CMK (downtime)
                 or dual-volumes + logical replication (zero downtime)
```

### Q6. You have a 500GB EBS gp2 volume and your database IOPS is half of what you expected. Why, and how do you fix it without overpaying?
**Answer:** The issue is gp2's IOPS-to-capacity ratio: gp2 gives 3 IOPS per GB, capped at 16,000 IOPS. A 500GB gp2 volume therefore provides 1,500 IOPS, not 16,000 — and that's the burst-bucket baseline. gp2 also has a burst bucket (up to 3,000 IOPS for small volumes) that depletes after sustained use, after which the volume drops to its baseline (1,500 IOPS for 500GB), which is exactly the half-throughput symptom you describe. The fix is to migrate to gp3, which decouples IOPS from capacity — a 500GB gp3 volume can be configured for any IOPS from 3,000 to 16,000 independent of size, at lower cost than gp2. The migration is a volume modification: `aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-type gp3 --iops 16000` — EBS performs an elastic modification in place, no downtime, takes a few minutes for the metadata change and longer for any IOPS expansion. The cost comparison: 500GB gp2 (1500 IOPS) is $50/month; 500GB gp3 at 16,000 IOPS is $40/month for storage + $80/month for IOPS = $120/month — but you can size to actual need; if you only need 6,000 IOPS, it's $40 + $30 = $70/month. The architectural lesson: gp2's capacity-tied IOPS is a pricing trap; always use gp3 for any workload where you need to control IOPS independently. For databases, monitor `VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps` and size gp3 IOPS to 2x peak to allow for bursts.
**Visual:**
```
gp2: 3 IOPS/GB -> 500GB = 1500 IOPS baseline (burst to 3000 then drains)
     symptom: starts fast, drops to 1500 after burst bucket empties
gp3: decoupled -> 500GB + 6000 IOPS = $70/mo (vs $50 gp2 with 1500 IOPS)
fix: modify-volume --volume-type gp3 --iops 6000 (no downtime, ~5min)
rule: never use gp2 for anything IOPS-sensitive
```

### Q7. You are designing the storage for a global multi-region financial trading database that requires sub-millisecond commit latency and zero data loss on regional failure. Is block storage the right choice, and how do you architect it?
**Answer:** Block storage alone cannot solve this — EBS is single-AZ, and even with multi-AZ replication it cannot provide cross-region synchronous replication at sub-millisecond latency (the speed of light between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 is ~50ms round-trip). The architecture must combine block storage with a higher-level replication layer. For sub-millisecond commits, the primary region runs on EBS io2 Block Express (sub-ms latency, 99.999% durability) with the database's WAL on the fastest tier. For zero data loss on regional failure, the database must do synchronous cross-region replication — but synchronous cross-region commits add 50–100ms of latency, which violates the sub-millisecond requirement. The resolution is to relax one constraint: either accept eventual cross-region consistency (async replication with RPO of seconds, using Aurora Global DB or PostgreSQL logical replication), or accept regional scope (synchronous replication only within a region, accept data loss if the whole region fails). For a financial trading system, the typical choice is the latter — synchronous replication within one region (EBS io2 + a synchronous standby in another AZ via database-level replication), with async replication to a DR region for disaster recovery (RPO of seconds, RTO of minutes). The lesson: sub-millisecond commits and zero cross-region data loss are physically incompatible due to the speed of light; pick one and design the system around the trade-off.
**Visual:**
```
EBS io2 BE in primary region, sub-ms commit
sync standby in 2nd AZ (database-level replication, <1ms)
async replicate to DR region (RPO seconds, RTO minutes)
speed of light: us-east-1 <-> eu-west-1 = 50ms RTT
                -> sync cross-region commit impossible at sub-ms
trade-off: pick (sub-ms + region-scoped) OR (global + eventual)
           financial trading: pick sub-ms + region-scoped, DR async
```

The mechanism is copy-on-write: when you trigger a snapshot, EBS briefly pauses writes, records the current state of every block's metadata, and resumes I/O; from that point forward, every block that is overwritten on the live volume is first copied to the snapshot store in S3.
